title: Psalm 69: Waters Up to the Neck
summary: A sufferer who is sinking in deep waters cries to God for rescue. He is hated without cause, shunned by his own family, and mocked because his zeal for God's house has cost him everything. He pleads for God's loving devotion, calls down judgment on those who poisoned his food and gave him vinegar, and ends by vowing thanksgiving and announcing that God will save Zion.
story: Psalm 69 sits near the end of Book II of the Psalter (Psalms 42 to 72), in a cluster of Davidic laments (Psalms 51 to 71) that closes with the royal prayer of Psalm 72. It is one of the longest individual laments in the book, and next to Psalms 22 and 110 it is among the psalms the New Testament quotes most often. The speaker is a faithful worshiper whose devotion has made him an outsider, a figure the Old Testament meets again in Jeremiah and in the suffering servant of Isaiah. The psalm's last verses widen from one man's rescue to the rebuilding of Zion and Judah, so the individual crisis becomes a window on the fortunes of the whole people.
historical:
The heading reads “For the choirmaster. To the tune of “Lilies.” Of David.” The phrase Of David (Hebrew ledavid) can mean by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, or dedicated to David, and scholars disagree on how much historical weight it carries. Traditional readers take the psalm as David's, written during one of the betrayals of his life, such as the rebellion of Absalom. Many modern scholars date it later, pointing to verses 35 and 36, which speak of God rebuilding the cities of Judah and his people settling there again. That language fits the time after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, and some think either the whole psalm or its closing lines come from the exile or the return. Others note that towns were sacked and rebuilt in many periods, and that a closing prayer for the nation could have been added when an older psalm was used in public worship.

The speaker's situation is concrete even if his name is not. He is a temple zealot mocked by elders at the gate and by drunks in the street, estranged from his brothers, accused of theft he did not commit, and forced to repay what he never took. Some scholars have compared him with Jeremiah, who was rejected by his own family, lowered into a muddy cistern, and ridiculed for his message about the temple (Jeremiah 12:6; 38:6). That comparison illustrates the type of figure the psalm describes rather than proving authorship.
cultural:
The gate was the public square of an Israelite town, where elders sat to hear cases, witness contracts, and pass judgment. To be the talk of “Those who sit at the gate” (verse 12) meant public disgrace before the community's leaders. Sackcloth, a rough cloth of goat hair, and fasting were ordinary signs of mourning and repentance; here even the speaker's grief becomes a joke.

The water imagery draws on the ancient fear of the deep. Mire, floods, and “the Pit” (verse 15) are pictures of death and the grave, the realm people went down into. Verse 21 describes an act of hostility, not hospitality: to offer poison or sour wine to a thirsty guest was to betray the most basic duty of the table. Verse 28 pictures a register of the living, a roll of citizens or of God's people, from which the wicked are to be removed (compare Exodus 32:32). Verse 31 echoes the prophetic conviction that God values a grateful heart above animal sacrifice, an ox or a bull with horns and hooves, the kind of animal the law declared clean and fit for the altar.
literary: The psalm moves through two rounds of lament and petition before turning to praise. Verses 1 to 4 describe drowning; verses 5 to 12 explain the cause, the speaker's zeal and the scorn it has brought; verses 13 to 18 plead for rescue in the same water language, so that the petition answers the complaint point by point. Verses 19 to 21 return to the insults and the cruel drink, and verses 22 to 28 form one of the strongest imprecations in the Psalter, a series of curses in which the enemies' punishment mirrors their crimes (their table, their eyes, their tents). Verse 29 turns sharply with “But I am in pain and distress”, and the psalm closes with a vow of praise (verses 30 to 33) and a call to heaven, earth, and sea to join it (verses 34 to 36). The key word is reproach (cherpah), which runs through the complaint like a drumbeat.

outline.t: Sinking in deep waters, hated without cause
Plea for rescue from the mire and the flood
No comforters, only gall and vinegar
A prayer for judgment on the persecutors
All creation praises the God who will save Zion

doctrines.note: The psalm describes the suffering of the righteous that comes precisely because of faithfulness. The speaker admits his own folly and guilt (verse 5), yet the scorn he bears is for God's sake, which gives believers words for pain that is not punishment.

Verses 22 to 28 hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it. The curses are fierce, but they are prayers, asking the judge of all the earth to act justly against those who persecute the one he has struck.

The speaker prays out of exhaustion, with a parched throat and failing eyes, and still grounds his plea in God's loving devotion and compassion. Honest prayer here includes confession, complaint, and a request for speed.

words.note: Cherpah, reproach, scorn, or disgrace. It appears five times in this psalm, more than any other significant word. It names public shame, the loss of honor before others, which in the ancient world could feel worse than physical pain. The speaker's reproach comes because he bears the insults aimed at God.

Qinah, zeal or jealousy. The word describes intense, exclusive passion, whether God's jealous love for his people or a person's burning devotion to God. In verse 9 zeal for God's house consumes the speaker, eating him up like fire.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love. It is God's covenant loyalty, love that keeps its promises. The speaker appeals to it twice (verses 13 and 16) as the ground of his hope when every human loyalty has failed.
Chomets, vinegar or sour wine. It was a cheap, soured wine, not a refreshing drink for a guest. Given to a thirsty man as mockery in verse 21, it becomes one of the psalm's most remembered details.

christ: The New Testament writers read this psalm as the voice of the righteous sufferer fulfilled in Jesus. When Jesus cleared the temple, his disciples remembered verse 9, that zeal for God's house would consume him (John 2:17). Jesus said that those who hated him did so without a cause, words found here in verse 4 and in Psalm 35:19 (John 15:25). Paul cites the second half of verse 9 to show that Christ did not please himself but bore the insults aimed at God (Romans 15:3). At the cross Jesus was offered wine mixed with gall and was given sour wine to drink, and John presents his cry of thirst as the fulfillment of Scripture (Matthew 27:34, 48; John 19:28-29). Peter applied verse 25 to Judas (Acts 1:20), and Paul applied verses 22 and 23 to the hardening of Israel (Romans 11:9-10). There is also a telling difference: the speaker confesses his folly and guilt, while Jesus, who took up his words, prayed for those who crucified him.

hard.q: How can a psalm that asks God to blot enemies out of the Book of Life be Scripture, especially when Jesus taught love for enemies?
hard.a: Psalm 69 is one of the imprecatory psalms, prayers that call down judgment. Several responses are offered by careful readers. One is that these prayers hand justice to God instead of taking revenge, which the law itself forbids (Leviticus 19:18); rage is brought into prayer rather than acted out. Another is that they voice the cry of the oppressed for justice, which God takes seriously and which reappears in the New Testament from the souls under the altar (Revelation 6:10). A third notes that the speaker is praying about persecutors of God's people and of God's own cause, not personal rivals. Christians also read these psalms in the light of the cross, where Jesus took the psalm's words of suffering on his lips but prayed for forgiveness for his enemies, showing that the hope of judgment and the offer of mercy now stand together. Readers differ on how directly Christians may pray these words today, but most agree they teach that injustice must be brought honestly to God.

questions: The speaker suffers because of his zeal for God, not because of wrongdoing. When has faithfulness cost you something with family or friends?
He admits his folly and guilt in verse 5 even while protesting his innocence toward his enemies. Why might both confessions belong in the same prayer?
What do you do with anger toward people who have wronged you, and how does praying it to God differ from acting it out?
